Where it began

Clive Lloyd was born in Georgetown, British Guiana, on 31 August 1944. At 16 he left school to work in the offices of the Georgetown hospital, and he played club cricket for Demerara. He first played for British Guiana in 1964.

As a boy he once watched from a tree outside the ground, with a view over the sightscreen, while Garry Sobers made two hundreds for West Indies against Pakistan. Cricket was in the family: the spin bowler Lance Gibbs was his cousin.

The player

He stood six feet five, with stooping shoulders and glasses, a powerful middle-order batter who bowled a little medium pace. His Test debut came against India in December 1966. In all he played 110 Tests between 1966 and 1984, scoring 7,515 runs at 46.68 with 19 hundreds and 39 fifties. His best was 242 not out against India at Mumbai in 1975, in a Test that decided the series.

He captained West Indies in 74 Tests, winning 36 and losing only 12. At one stage his side went 27 matches without defeat, including 11 wins in a row. He also led them to World Cup wins in 1975 and 1979. In the 1975 final at Lord's he came in at 50 for 3 and made 102 from 85 balls, and West Indies beat Australia by 17 runs on the longest day's play the ground had known.

What made him special

As a captain he could see what his side might become. After a heavy series defeat in Australia in 1975–76 he built his team around fast bowling, and Michael Holding, Andy Roberts, Joel Garner and Colin Croft gave West Indies a run of success they had never had before. He hooked Dennis Lillee for six in that 1975 final and struck 70 sixes in Tests.

His bowling was a gentler business. Ten Test wickets at 62.20 suggest he was used sparingly, although he did take a wicket with his very first ball in one-day internationals, the first West Indian to do so.

Away from the middle

England came to know him well. He played league cricket for Haslingden and then joined Lancashire, where he stayed from 1968 to 1986 and was made captain in 1981. In 1970 he helped them win both the John Player League and the Gillette Cup. He followed Everton.

After playing he managed West Indies in the late 1990s, coached, commentated and was a match referee for the ICC between 2001 and 2006. He was a Wisden Cricketer of the Year in 1971, and in 1985 Australia made him honorary Officer of the Order of Australia. He joined the ICC Cricket Hall of Fame in 2009. The 2020 New Year Honours brought a knighthood for his services to the game.

And finally

He first watched Test cricket from the branches of a tree outside the ground. He went on to watch a great deal more of it from the middle, as captain of one of the finest sides the game has seen, which counts as a considerable upgrade in seating.
